questions.question_text: In Virginia designated agency, who assigns separate licensees to represent each party in a transaction?
distractors: The managing broker
The listing agent
The Virginia REB
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 54.1-2139.1 lets the principal or supervising broker assign different licensees in the firm to represent different clients in the same transaction. Virginia calls them designated agents or designated representatives.

questions.question_text: A buyer and seller are both clients of the same brokerage. The principal broker designates separate agents for each. What role does the principal broker hold?
questions.correct_answer: Dual agent who supervises both sides
distractors: Neutral third-party mediator
Designated agent for the seller only
Transaction coordinator with no duties
questions.explanation: Under Va. Code § 54.1-2139.1 the broker who makes the designation remains a dual agent or dual representative and supervises both sides, and the required written disclosure must say so. The broker must ensure confidential information is not passed between the designated licensees.

questions.question_text: Agent Kim is designated to represent the buyer and Agent Lee represents the seller in the same firm. Kim learns the buyer will pay $20,000 over asking. What must Kim do?
questions.correct_answer: Keep it confidential from Agent Lee
distractors: Disclose it to the principal broker only
Share it with Lee for fair dealing
Report it to the Virginia REB
questions.explanation: Each designated agent owes the full duties of a standard agent to their own client, including confidentiality under Va. Code § 54.1-2131 and § 54.1-2132. A buyer's willingness to pay more must not be shared with the licensee designated for the seller.

questions.question_text: Before designated agency can begin in Virginia, what must be obtained from both parties?
distractors: Verbal acknowledgment from each party
A signed waiver of fiduciary duties
Approval from the Virginia REB
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 54.1-2139.1 requires written disclosure to, and written acknowledgment from, all clients — identifying which licensee represents which party and stating that the supervising broker remains a dual representative — before designated representation begins.

questions.question_text: What level of duty does each designated agent owe to their assigned client in Virginia?
distractors: Limited advisory duties only
Ministerial duties only
Duties of honesty and fair dealing
questions.explanation: Each designated licensee owes their assigned client the duties of the representation named in the brokerage agreement; for a standard agent that is the full statutory set in Va. Code § 54.1-2131/2132 — promoting the client's interests, confidentiality, ordinary care, accounting, and disclosure of material facts. That is what distinguishes designated representation from one licensee acting as a dual representative.

questions.question_text: A Virginia agent represents both buyer and seller in the same transaction. Which statement best describes this arrangement?
questions.correct_answer: It is dual agency requiring written consent
distractors: It is prohibited under Virginia law
It requires only verbal agreement
It converts the agent to a facilitator
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 54.1-2139 permits dual agency or dual representation in residential transactions only with the written consent of all parties, given after written disclosure of the consequences and before the dual representation begins.

questions.question_text: Agent Patel is a dual agent. The seller privately says she would accept $15,000 less than the listing price. What should Agent Patel do?
distractors: Share it with the buyer immediately
Disclose it if asked directly by the buyer
Report it to the principal broker
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 54.1-2139 F bars a dual agent from disclosing information given in the confidence and trust of the brokerage relationship with the other client. A seller's bottom line is exactly that, so it stays confidential.

questions.question_text: Which action is prohibited for a dual agent in Virginia?
questions.correct_answer: Advising either party on the terms to offer or accept
distractors: Presenting all offers to the seller
Providing market data to both parties
Preparing documents for both parties
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 54.1-2139 spells out what a dual representative may not do: advise either party on what terms to offer or accept, advise the buyer on the suitability or condition of the property, or advise either party in a dispute arising from the transaction. The licensee may still perform ministerial acts and provide factual information to both sides.

questions.question_text: In a dual agency situation, Agent Torres knows the buyer's maximum price and the seller's minimum price. Which is Torres permitted to disclose?
distractors: Both prices to both parties
The buyer's maximum to the seller
The seller's minimum to the buyer
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 54.1-2139 F protects information each client gave in the confidence and trust of the brokerage relationship. Neither party's price limit may be revealed to the other.

questions.question_text: A buyer refuses to sign a dual agency consent form. What must the agent do?
questions.correct_answer: Not proceed as a dual agent
distractors: Continue with implied consent
Have the seller sign for both parties
Proceed if verbally acknowledged
questions.explanation: Dual representation requires the written consent of all parties under Va. Code § 54.1-2139. Without it the licensee cannot proceed as a dual representative, and the statute expressly allows the licensee to withdraw without liability from representing a client who refuses to consent.

questions.question_text: A buyer chooses not to enter a representation agreement with any agent. Under Virginia law, what is this buyer's status?
distractors: A client with full fiduciary rights
An unprotected party with no rights
A subagent of the listing broker
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 54.1-2130 defines a customer as a person who has not entered into a brokerage relationship but for whom the licensee performs ministerial acts. The licensee owes honesty, disclosure of material adverse facts about the property's physical condition, and accounting for money — not fiduciary-level duties.

questions.question_text: Agent Brooks is working with an unrepresented buyer at an open house. Brooks discovers the home has a cracked foundation. What must Brooks do?
distractors: Say nothing since there is no agency
Only disclose if the buyer asks directly
Refer the buyer to a home inspector
questions.explanation: Brooks is at the seller's open house, so Va. Code § 54.1-2131 B applies: a seller's agent must disclose to prospective buyers all material adverse facts pertaining to the physical condition of the property that are actually known, whether or not the buyer is a client.

questions.question_text: Which fiduciary duty does a Virginia agent owe to an unrepresented customer?
distractors: Loyalty to the customer
Obedience to customer instructions
Confidentiality of all information
questions.explanation: Fiduciary-level duties belong to clients. A customer is owed honesty, no knowingly false information, disclosure of material adverse facts about the property's physical condition, and accounting for money and property (Va. Code § 54.1-2131 B).

questions.question_text: An agent receives a $5,000 earnest money deposit from an unrepresented buyer. What duty applies to these funds?
distractors: No duty since there is no agency
Hold funds in the agent's personal account
Return the deposit within 24 hours
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 54.1-2131 B requires accounting for money and property received from any party, and 18VAC135-20-181 requires it to go into the firm's escrow account. The duty does not depend on an agency relationship.

questions.question_text: When working with an unrepresented party, what must a Virginia licensee clearly communicate?
questions.correct_answer: That the party is not being represented
distractors: That dual agency has been established
That the agent works as a facilitator
That fiduciary duties still apply
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 54.1-2138 requires written, conspicuous disclosure of the licensee's brokerage relationship to any buyer or seller who is not the licensee's client and is not represented by another licensee, so the party understands the licensee does not represent them.
